Beyond SGD, Without SVD:
Proximal Subspace Iteration LoRA with Diagonal Fractional K-FAC

Abdulla Jasem Almansoori Affiliation: MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi, UAE Correspondence to: abdulla.almansoori@mbzuai.ac.ae    Maria Ivanova Affiliation: Yandex School of Data Analysis, Moscow, Russia    Andrey Veprikov Affiliation: MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi, UAE Affiliation: SB AI Lab, Moscow, Russia Affiliation: Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence (MIRAI), Moscow, Russia Affiliation: Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab), Moscow, Russia    Aleksandr Beznosikov Affiliation: Moscow Independent Research Institute of Artificial Intelligence (MIRAI), Moscow, Russia Affiliation: Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab), Moscow, Russia    Samuel Horváth Affiliation: MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi, UAE    Martin Takáč Affiliation: MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi, UAE
Abstract

Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tunes large models by learning low-rank updates on top of frozen weights, dramatically reducing trainable parameters and memory (Hu et al., 2022). In this work, we address the gap between training with full steps with low-rank projections (SVDLoRA) and LoRA fine-tuning. We propose LoRSum, a memory-efficient subroutine that closes this gap for gradient descent by casting LoRA optimization as a proximal sub-problem and solving it efficiently with alternating least squares updates, which we prove to be an implicit block power method. We recover several recently proposed preconditioning methods for LoRA as special cases, and show that LoRSum can also be used for updating a low-rank momentum. In order to address full steps with preconditioned gradient descent, we propose a scaled variant of LoRSum that uses structured metrics such as K-FAC and Shampoo, and we show that storing the diagonal of these metrics still allows them to perform well while remaining memory-efficient. Experiments on a synthetic task, CIFAR-100, and language-model fine-tuning on GLUE, SQuAD v2, and WikiText-103, show that our method can match or improve LoRA baselines given modest compute overhead, while avoiding full-matrix SVD projections and retaining LoRA-style parameter efficiency.11 1 Code: https://github.com/zeligism/PSI-LoRA

Keywords: 
Optimization, LoRA, Low-rank, alternating least squares, SVD, K-FAC, Natural Gradient, Memory-efficient
††affiliationnotice: Equal contribution

1 Introduction

Fine-tuning large pretrained models remains costly as updating all parameters demands substantial GPU memory and state tracking. Parameter-efficient methods like LoRA replace full fine-tuning with low-rank adapters 𝐔∈ℝdout×r\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times r}, 𝐕∈ℝdin×r\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}\times r} added to a frozen base weight 𝐖base\mathbf{W}^{\text{base}} so that 𝐖tuned=𝐖base+𝐔𝐕⊤\mathbf{W}^{\text{tuned}}=\mathbf{W}^{\text{base}}+\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top} with r≪min⁡(dout,din)r\ll\min(d_{\text{out}},d_{\text{in}}) (Hu et al., 2022). Although LoRA reduces parameter and memory costs, first-order training of (𝐔,𝐕)(\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}) can be ill-conditioned (Tong et al., 2021) and sensitive to hyperparameters. Preconditioning with 𝐕⊤​𝐕\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{V} and 𝐔⊤​𝐔\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{U} remedies part of this (Zhang & Pilanci, 2024; Zhang et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2021), yet each step still acts only locally on the current factor subspaces.

As an oracle baseline, consider taking a full step in weight space 𝐖←𝐖+Δ\mathbf{W}\leftarrow\mathbf{W}+\Delta, and then projecting it back to rank rr w.r.t. the Frobenius norm. We refer to this baseline as SVDLoRA because by Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem, the optimal rank-rr projection is given by the truncated SVD of 𝐖+Δ\mathbf{W}+\Delta. While this does not guarantee maximal objective decrease for a non-quadratic loss, it cleanly isolates the optimization gap introduced by enforcing rank rr after a full update. Indeed, this has been recently proposed as an initialization scheme for LoRA-One (Zhang et al., 2025), so one can imagine that reapplying this projection each step would yield the best possible LoRA performance. But this is clearly costly in terms of both compute and memory since it requires running an SVD every step on a dout×dind_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}} matrix. Nonetheless, the existence of the rank-rr updates themselves—the difference between the current weights and their rank-rr SVD projection—suggests that we can do better.

In this work, we propose LoRSum (Low-Rank Sum), a stable and memory-efficient subroutine for finding the best rank-rr solution to a sum of low-rank matrices. The utility of LoRSum lies in its ability to approximate the above SVD baseline without forming or operating on the full matrix, which is inspired from the observation that the gradient 𝐆\mathbf{G} in LoRA admits a memory-efficient factorization based on the input and output gradients of the layer. The derivation of LoRSum is simple and follows from casting the SVD of an update as a proximal sub-problem in LoRA parameter space. The solution uses alternating least squares (ALS) to approximate the solution iteratively, which we prove to be a block power method implicitly. In addition to approximating the full update, LoRSum can also be used for updating low-rank approximations of the momentum buffers efficiently. We further show that LoRSum can recover many existing methods in the literature (Tong et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023a; Xu et al., 2023; Zhang & Pilanci, 2024) as special cases.

When the step Δ\Delta is not expressible as a sum of low-rank terms, such as in preconditioned gradient descent like Adam (Kingma & Ba, 2017) or natural gradient descent (Amari, 1998), the standard LoRSum is no longer directly applicable. In order to address this important case, we propose F-LoRSum (Fisher-metric LoRSum), which is a memory-efficient scaled variant that uses Kronecker-factored metrics like K-FAC (Martens & Grosse, 2020) and Shampoo (Gupta et al., 2018) to scale the updates. In general, Kronecker-factored metrics are not memory-efficient for LoRA training since they require storing full din×dind_{\text{in}}\times d_{\text{in}} and dout×doutd_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{out}} matrices. However, our implementation only requires storing their diagonal approximations, which ultimately makes F-LoRSum’s memory storage requirements even less than Adam’s. Indeed, F-LoRSum with rank-11 momentum and diagonal metrics needs an extra memory of 2​(din+dout)2(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}}), whereas Adam requires an extra memory of 2​r​(din+dout)2r(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}}) for the first and second moments. Compare with the memory-efficient AdaFactor (Shazeer & Stern, 2018) which requires (din+dout)(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}}) extra memory for the second moment. Still, we show in the experiments that, not only does F-LoRSum remain memory-efficient, it can even outperform full-tuned Adam baseline on some GLUE tasks (Wang et al., 2019).

Contributions.

We make the following contributions:

  1. 1.

    LoRSum: a stable and memory-efficient subroutine for approximating the best proximal rank-rr sum of low-rank matrices, which we used to approximate the SVD a full update and full momentum. We show that LoRSum recovers existing preconditioned LoRA methods as special cases, and prove in Theorem 3.1 that LoRSum is a subspace iteration method that converges to SVDLoRA as the number of inner iterations KK increases, as shown in Figure 1.

  2. 2.

    F-LoRSum: a LoRSum variant for preconditioned steps with Kronecker-factored metrics.

  3. 3.

    PSI-LoRA and Scaled PSI-LoRA, two practical and memory-efficient optimizers based on the subroutines LoRSum and F-LoRSum, with full reference implementations in Appendix E.

  4. 4.

    Show empirical gains and learning rate robustness over LoRA baselines on linear synthetic task, CIFAR-100, GLUE, SQuAD v2, and WikiText-103.

Setup and notation.

For a single layer with frozen 𝐖base∈ℝdout×din\mathbf{W}^{\text{base}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}}, we learn rank-rr adapters 𝐔∈ℝdout×r\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times r} and 𝐕∈ℝdin×r\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}\times r}, so that the effective tuned weight at iteration tt is 𝐖ttuned=𝐖base+𝐔t​𝐕t⊤\mathbf{W}_{t}^{\text{tuned}}=\mathbf{W}^{\text{base}}+\mathbf{U}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}. Henceforth, we make the dependence on 𝐖base\mathbf{W}^{\text{base}} implicit as it does not affect our analysis. We define the low-rank matrix formed by the adapter as 𝐖t:=𝐔t​𝐕t⊤\mathbf{W}_{t}:=\mathbf{U}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}.

Let f⁡(𝐖t)f(\mathbf{W}_{t}) be the objective and define the full gradient 𝐆t:=∇𝐖f​(𝐖t)\mathbf{G}_{t}:=\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}f(\mathbf{W}_{t}), which is also equal to the gradient w.r.t. 𝐖ttuned\mathbf{W}_{t}^{\text{tuned}}. By the chain rule, 𝐆𝐔,t=∇𝐔f​(𝐖t)=𝐆t​𝐕t\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{U},t}=\nabla_{\mathbf{U}}f(\mathbf{W}_{t})=\mathbf{G}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t} and 𝐆𝐕,t=∇𝐕f​(𝐖t)=𝐆t⊤​𝐔t\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{V},t}=\nabla_{\mathbf{V}}f(\mathbf{W}_{t})=\mathbf{G}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}_{t}. Fix a linear layer, and let 𝐗t∈ℝB×din\mathbf{X}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times d_{\text{in}}} be the inputs and 𝐒t=∇(𝐖𝐗)⊤f​(𝐖)∈ℝB×dout\mathbf{S}_{t}=\nabla_{(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{X})^{\top}}f(\mathbf{W})\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times d_{\text{out}}} be the gradients w.r.t. its outputs, where BB is the effective batch size. Then, 𝐆t=𝐒t⊤​𝐗t\mathbf{G}_{t}=\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}. We exploit this factorized structure to perform only thin GEMM operations.

2 Related Work

Preconditioned optimization for fixed-rank parameterizations. Prior work improves the conditioning of low-rank factor optimization by preconditioning factor gradients, leading to updates that depend on 𝐕⊤​𝐕\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{V} and 𝐔⊤​𝐔\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{U} (Tong et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023a; Xu et al., 2023). Riemannian preconditioned LoRA derives analogous updates from fixed-rank manifold geometry (Zhang & Pilanci, 2024). We instead view LoRA training as approximately solving the rank-rr projection of a full (possibly preconditioned) step. One simultaneous iteration recovers these methods, while additional alternating iterations refine toward the best rank-rr direction.

Projection and SVD-based low-rank updates. Projecting a dense update back to rank rr via truncated SVD (our SVDLoRA oracle) is the optimal Frobenius-norm rank-rr projection, but it is typically too expensive for large layers. This motivates iterative low-rank approximation (e.g., subspace iteration) and incremental SVD updates (Brand, 2006). Our LoRSum can be seen as a warm-started subspace-iteration approximation that uses only thin operations and exploits gradient factorization. Related in spirit, GaLore projects gradients to a low-dimensional subspace (Zhao et al., 2024). We instead target the rank-rr projection of a full step, with KK controlling projection accuracy.

LoRA variants, reparameterizations, and initialization. A number of works modify LoRA or its training protocol to improve efficiency or generalization. AdaLoRA adapts rank allocation using SVD-inspired criteria (Zhang et al., 2023b), while DoRA reparameterizes weights into magnitude and direction and adapts both components (Liu et al., 2024). Other methods periodically merge adapters into the base weights or change the adapter schedule (Lialin et al., 2023). Several approaches focus on improving optimization through initialization or local geometry. PiSSA initializes LoRA adapters using leading singular directions of pretrained weights (Meng et al., 2024), and LoRA-Pro uses a higher-dimensional tangent space to derive improved updates (Wang et al., 2025). Particularly close in motivation is LoRA-One. It uses an SVD-based initialization associated with projecting a full step (SVDLoRA) and then applies preconditioned factor updates (Zhang et al., 2025). Our contribution is complementary because rather than changing the adapter or relying on periodic SVD resets, we provide a memory-efficient subroutine that approximates the rank-rr projected step itself.

Optimizer state under rank constraints and Fisher-structured scaling. Maintaining optimizer state (e.g. momentum) in low-rank training is nontrivial because naive momentum accumulates past gradients that generally do not lie in the current factor subspaces. LoFT addresses this by projecting momentum-like quantities onto iterates’ subspaces, which can restrict momentum to joint subspaces across time (Tastan et al., 2025). Recent work also proposes maintaining explicit low-rank factorizations of momentum matrices (Mahdavinia & Mahdavi, 2025). In our approach, the same LoRSum routine used for projected steps can also be used to maintain a low-rank estimate of momentum in Frobenius norm. Moreover, we incorporate curvature information through Fisher/Kronecker-structured metrics. K-FAC approximates the natural-gradient metric using Kronecker-factored Fisher blocks (Heskes, 2000; Martens & Grosse, 2020), and Shampoo uses Kronecker-structured second moments with fractional matrix powers (Gupta et al., 2018). We endow our projection subproblem with such metrics (and practical diagonal approximations), yielding scaled variants of LoRSum and PSI-LoRA.

How our work is positioned. Overall, we provide a reusable, SVD-free projection subroutine for approximating full steps and low-rank state updates within standard LoRA fine-tuning.

3 Without SVD: Proximal Subspace Iteration LoRA

In this section, we derive LoRSum, a memory-efficient subroutine for approximating the best rank-rr projection of a full step, and describe PSI-LoRA (Proximal Subspace Iteration LoRA), a LoRA optimizer that uses LoRSum to approximate SVDLoRA steps and low-rank momentum.

Let 𝐖t:=𝐔t​𝐕t⊤\mathbf{W}_{t}:=\mathbf{U}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top} denote the LoRA at the current step. We can derive the ideal gradient descent in adapter space as a projected gradient step

=arg​minrank⁡(𝐖)≤r⁡12​‖𝐖−(𝐖t−η​𝐆t)‖F2\displaystyle=\argmin_{\rank(\mathbf{W})\leq r}\,\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{W}-(\mathbf{W}_{t}-\eta\mathbf{G}_{t})\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}

For any matrix 𝐖¯t+1:=𝐖t+Δ\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}:=\mathbf{W}_{t}+\Delta, the Frobenius-norm best rank-rr approximation Πr​(𝐖¯t+1)∈arg​minrank⁡(𝐖)≤r⁡‖𝐖−𝐖¯t+1‖F\Pi_{r}(\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1})\in\argmin_{\rank(\mathbf{W})\leq r}\|\mathbf{W}-\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\|_{\mathrm{F}} is given by the rank-rr truncated SVD of 𝐖¯t+1\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}.

We know that 𝐖t\mathbf{W}_{t} is low-rank by construction, so our goal is to approximate Πr​(𝐖t+Δ)\Pi_{r}(\mathbf{W}_{t}+\Delta) given a step Δ\Delta without forming Δ\Delta as a dense dout×dind_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}} matrix or running a truncated SVD each step.

3.2 Approximating rank-rr projections via warm-started ALS

In the gradient descent case, 𝐖¯t+1=𝐖t+Δ\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}=\mathbf{W}_{t}+\Delta admits a memory-efficient representation since Δ=−η​𝐆t=−η​𝐒t⊤​𝐗t\Delta=-\eta\mathbf{G}_{t}=-\eta\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}. Thus, we can write 𝐖¯t+1=𝐔t​𝐕t⊤−η​𝐒t⊤​𝐗t\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}=\mathbf{U}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}-\eta\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t} as a sum of two low-rank matrices.

We now consider a regularized low-rank projection of 𝐖¯t+1\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1} the standard rank-rr factorized space (𝐔,𝐕)(\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V})

When 𝐖¯t+1=𝐔t​𝐕t⊤−η​𝐆t\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}=\mathbf{U}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}-\eta\mathbf{G}_{t} and λ\lambda is a small damping term, dropping the mild shrinkage factors yields the familiar preconditioned factor updates

which corresponds to ScaledGD(λ\lambda) (Tong et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2023) and Riemannian preconditioned LoRA (with λ\lambda used as practical damping) (Zhang & Pilanci, 2024). PrecGD uses a similar update but with adaptive damping instead (Zhang et al., 2021), but we do not consider it for simplicity. However, see Section A.2 for an interesting connection.

The form 7 is particularly appealing and easy to implement since 𝐆𝐔,t\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{U},t} and 𝐆𝐕,t\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{V},t} are already computed by automatic differentiation (autograd) and it only requires inverting small r×rr\times r matrices. In addition to the fact that 7 is an approximation, extending 6 to multiple inner iterations via autograd alone is not possible. The full gradients 𝐆t=𝐒t⊤​𝐗t\mathbf{G}_{t}=\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t} are not stored by autograd, so we need backward hooks to save 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} and 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t} in order to compute quantities such as 𝐆t​𝐕(k+1)\mathbf{G}_{t}{\mathbf{V}^{(k+1)}}, whereas a normal backward pass can only compute 𝐆t​𝐕t=𝐆t​𝐕(0)\mathbf{G}_{t}{\mathbf{V}_{t}}=\mathbf{G}_{t}{\mathbf{V}^{(0)}}.

3.3 LoRSum as proximal rank-rr projections.

In practice, we found that the factor regularization 3 can sometimes be unstable and leads to diverging updates. In order to control the updates themselves, we consider a proximal regularizer w.r.t. (𝐔t,𝐕t)(\mathbf{U}_{t},\mathbf{V}_{t}) instead

ℛprox​(𝐔,𝐕)=ρ2​(‖𝐔−𝐔t‖F2+‖𝐕−𝐕t‖F2).\mathcal{R}_{\text{prox}}(\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V})=\frac{\rho}{2}(\left\|\mathbf{U}-\mathbf{U}_{t}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}+\left\|\mathbf{V}-\mathbf{V}_{t}\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}). (8)

Then, the subproblem 2 under the proximal regularizer becomes

arg​min𝐔,𝐕\displaystyle\argmin_{\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}} 12​‖𝐔𝐕⊤−(𝐔t​𝐕t⊤−η​𝐆t)‖F2\displaystyle\tfrac{1}{2}\|{\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}}-({\mathbf{U}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}}-\eta\mathbf{G}_{t})\|^{2}_{\mathrm{F}} (9)
+ρ2​‖𝐔−𝐔t‖F2+ρ2​‖𝐕−𝐕t‖F2\displaystyle+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|{\mathbf{U}}-{\mathbf{U}_{t}}\|^{2}_{\mathrm{F}}{+\tfrac{\rho}{2}\|\mathbf{V}-\mathbf{V}_{t}\|^{2}_{\mathrm{F}}}
=arg​min𝐔,𝐕\displaystyle=\argmin_{\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}} ⟨𝐔𝐕⊤,𝐆t⟩F+12​η​‖𝐔𝐕⊤−𝐔t​𝐕t⊤‖F2\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top},\mathbf{G}_{t}\rangle_{\mathrm{F}}+\tfrac{1}{2\eta}\|{\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}}-{\mathbf{U}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}}\|^{2}_{\mathrm{F}}
+ρ2​η​‖𝐔−𝐔t‖F2+ρ2​η​‖𝐕−𝐕t‖F2.\displaystyle+\tfrac{\rho}{2\eta}\|{\mathbf{U}}-{\mathbf{U}_{t}}\|^{2}_{\mathrm{F}}{+\tfrac{\rho}{2\eta}\|\mathbf{V}-\mathbf{V}_{t}\|^{2}_{\mathrm{F}}}.

This construction can offer two interpretations: (i) a proximal rank-rr projection of the full step 𝐖t+1=𝐖t−η​𝐆t\mathbf{W}_{t+1}=\mathbf{W}_{t}-\eta\mathbf{G}_{t}, where the proximal term penalizes large deviations in LoRA space from the current step (𝐔t,𝐕t)(\mathbf{U}_{t},\mathbf{V}_{t}), and (ii) a proximal update in a lifted space (𝐖,𝐔,𝐕)(\mathbf{W},\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}) on the linearized objective f⁡(𝐖)≈f⁡(𝐖t)+⟨𝐆t,𝐖−𝐖t⟩f(\mathbf{W})\approx f(\mathbf{W}_{t})+\langle\mathbf{G}_{t},\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{t}\rangle, under the non-linear constraint 𝐖=𝐔𝐕⊤\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}. See Appendix C for further discussion.

Proximal ALS updates.

Given the proximal regularizer 8, the Gauss-Seidel iterations that approximately solve 9 are given by

𝐔(k+1)\displaystyle\mathbf{U}^{(k+1)} ←(𝐖¯t+1​𝐕(k)+ρ​𝐔t)​((𝐕(k))⊤​𝐕(k)+ρ​𝐈)−1,\displaystyle\leftarrow\big(\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}+\rho\,\mathbf{U}_{t}\big)\Big((\mathbf{V}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}+\rho\mathbf{I}\Big)^{-1}, (10)
𝐕(k+1)\displaystyle\mathbf{V}^{(k+1)} ←(𝐖¯t+1⊤​𝐔(k+1)+ρ​𝐕t)​((𝐔(k+1))⊤​𝐔(k+1)+ρ​𝐈)−1.\displaystyle\leftarrow\big(\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}^{\top}\mathbf{U}^{(k+1)}+\rho\,\mathbf{V}_{t}\big)\Big((\mathbf{U}^{(k+1)})^{\top}\mathbf{U}^{(k+1)}+\rho\mathbf{I}\Big)^{-1}.

The additional proximal terms (ρ​𝐔t,ρ​𝐕t\rho\mathbf{U}_{t},\rho\mathbf{V}_{t}) can seem like a small improvement, but we found them to be important for the stability of the updates.

Low-Rank Sum (LoRSum)

More generally, suppose we are given the next step as a sum of low-rank matrices

𝐖¯t+1=∑j=1ncj​𝐔j​𝐕j⊤,\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{j}\,\mathbf{U}_{j}\mathbf{V}_{j}^{\top},

and we want a rank-rr approximation represented by factors (𝐔,𝐕)(\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}), warm-started at (𝐔1,𝐕1)(\mathbf{U}_{1},\mathbf{V}_{1}). We define LoRSum as (approximately) solving the proximal projection

min𝐔,𝐕⁡12​‖𝐔𝐕⊤−𝐖¯t+1‖F2+ρ2​(‖𝐔−𝐔1‖F2+‖𝐕−𝐕1‖F2),\min_{\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}}\;\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}-\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}+\frac{\rho}{2}\Big(\|\mathbf{U}-\mathbf{U}_{1}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}+\|\mathbf{V}-\mathbf{V}_{1}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\Big),

with KK Gauss-Seidel ALS iterations, yielding the same updates in 10 but with 𝐖¯t+1=∑j=1ncj​𝐔j​𝐕j⊤\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{j}\,\mathbf{U}_{j}\mathbf{V}_{j}^{\top}. These updates define our LoRSum subroutine, written as 𝐖t+1=LoRSum​(∑j=1ncj​𝐔j,t​𝐕j,t⊤,K,ρ)\mathbf{W}_{t+1}=\textsc{LoRSum}(\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{j}\mathbf{U}_{j,t}\mathbf{V}_{j,t}^{\top};\,K,\rho). We show a simplified procedure in Algorithm 1. For the full details, please refer to Appendix E.

The careful reader may note that by stacking [𝐔1,t+1​…​𝐔n,t+1]​[𝐕1,t+1​…​𝐕n,t+1]⊤[\mathbf{U}_{1,t+1}\ldots\mathbf{U}_{n,t+1}][\mathbf{V}_{1,t+1}\ldots\mathbf{V}_{n,t+1}]^{\top}, we can instead perform a low-rank modification to a previously-obtained SVD (Brand, 2006), which requires one SVD at initialization and then thin operations afterwards. However, the benefit of introducing LoRSum is that we can reuse the efficient subroutine in 5 to sum low-rank matrices under two practical knobs: KK for controlling approximation accuracy and ρ\rho for controlling update stability. Both of these properties are desirable for low-rank updates to be fast and stable enough for deep learning applications.

Subspace iteration.

Let 𝒫𝐗:=𝐗​(𝐗⊤​𝐗)†​𝐗⊤\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{X}}:=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{\dagger}\mathbf{X}^{\top} be the projection onto the column space of 𝐗\mathbf{X}, where † denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. Consider the fixed-point equations in 4 with λ=0\lambda=0, and observe that by right-multiplying 𝐔\mathbf{U}’s update by 𝐕⊤\mathbf{V}^{\top} and left-multiplying 𝐕\mathbf{V}’s update by 𝐔⊤\mathbf{U}^{\top}, we can write them as projections

𝐔𝐕⊤=𝐖¯t+1​𝒫𝐕=𝒫𝐔​𝐖¯t+1.\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}=\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{V}}=\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{U}}\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}. (11)

Under the alternating updates in 10 with ρ=0\rho=0 (or equivalently 5 with λ=0\lambda=0), these projections can be seen as block power iterations on 𝐖¯t+1⊤​𝐖¯t+1\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}^{\top}\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1} and 𝐖¯t+1​𝐖¯t+1⊤\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}^{\top}.

Theorem 3.1 (LoRSum as a warm-started subspace iteration).

Consider the iterations 10, where 𝐖¯t+1=𝐔t(0)​𝐕t(0)−η​𝐆t\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}=\mathbf{U}_{t}^{(0)}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{(0)}-\eta\mathbf{G}_{t} and ρ=0\rho=0. Assume span⁡(𝐕(0))\mathspan(\mathbf{V}^{(0)}) has nonzero overlap with the top-rr right singular subspace of 𝐖¯t+1\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}. Let σ1≥…​σmin⁡{din,dout}\sigma_{1}\geq\ldots\sigma_{\min\{d_{\text{in}},d_{\text{out}}\}} be the singular values of 𝐖¯t+1\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1} and let 𝐖t+1svd=Πr​(𝐖¯t+1)\mathbf{W}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{svd}}=\Pi_{r}(\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}) be its best rank-rr approximation. Then, for some constant C>0C>0 that depends on the initialization 𝐕t(0)\mathbf{V}_{t}^{(0)}, we have that

‖𝐔t(k)​𝐕t(k)−𝐖t+1svd‖F2≤C​(σr+1σr)2​k.\|\mathbf{U}_{t}^{(k)}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{(k)}-\mathbf{W}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{svd}}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\leq C\left(\frac{\sigma_{r+1}}{\sigma_{r}}\right)^{2k}.

The proof uses a standard argument for subspace iteration and is deferred to Appendix B for brevity.

3.4 Momentum with LoRSum

Let ℳ⁡(𝐆𝐔)\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{U}}) and ℳ⁡(𝐆𝐕)\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{V}}) be the momentum buffers for the LoRA gradients, and consider only ℳ⁡(𝐆𝐔)\mathcal{M}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{U}}) for brevity. A naive implementation is to accumulate the preconditioned gradients

ℳtnaive​(𝐆𝐔):=𝐆𝐔,t​(𝐕t⊤​𝐕t)−1+α​ℳt−1naive​(𝐆𝐔).\mathcal{M}_{t}^{\text{naive}}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{U}}):=\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{U},t}(\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{V}_{t})^{-1}+\alpha\mathcal{M}_{t-1}^{\text{naive}}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{U}}).

This does not preserve the property in 11 as the buffers contain stale inverse gram matrices. An intuitive fix is to re-project the momentum buffers before preconditioning LoFT (Tastan et al., 2025).

ℳtproj​(𝐆𝐔)\displaystyle\mathcal{M}_{t}^{\text{proj}}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{U}}) :=𝐆𝐔,t​(𝐕t⊤​𝐕t)−1\displaystyle:=\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{U},t}(\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{V}_{t})^{-1}
+α​ℳt−1proj​(𝐆𝐔)​𝐕t−1⊤​𝐕t​(𝐕t⊤​𝐕t)−1\displaystyle\quad+\alpha\mathcal{M}_{t-1}^{\text{proj}}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{U}})\mathbf{V}_{t-1}^{\top}\mathbf{V}_{t}(\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{V}_{t})^{-1}
ℳtproj​(𝐆𝐔)​𝐕t⊤\displaystyle{\color[rgb]{0.4,0,0}\mathcal{M}_{t}^{\text{proj}}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{U}})\mathbf{V}_{t}^{\top}} =(𝐆t+α​ℳt−1proj​(𝐆𝐔)​𝐕t−1⊤)​𝒫𝐕t,\displaystyle=(\mathbf{G}_{t}+\alpha{\color[rgb]{0.4,0,0}\mathcal{M}_{t-1}^{\text{proj}}(\mathbf{G}_{\mathbf{U}})\mathbf{V}_{t-1}^{\top}})\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{V}_{t}},

However, this iteratively projects the buffer onto the joint subspace of all iterations. In addition, it requires saving the previous iterates.

Instead of maintaining factor-space momentum like LoFT, we propose to maintain momentum in the full weight space using LoRSum. We initialize a zero rank-rmr_{m} momentum matrix as in LoRA (to satisfy the warm-start condition in Theorem 3.1), and use the LoRSum subroutine to update it to get the best estimate under the Frobenius norm.

ℳtlor:=LoRSum​(α​ℳt−1lor​(𝐆)+𝐆t).\mathcal{M}_{t}^{\text{lor}}:=\textsc{LoRSum}(\alpha\mathcal{M}_{t-1}^{\text{lor}}(\mathbf{G})+\mathbf{G}_{t}). (12)

This has memory cost O⁡((din+dout)​rm)O((d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})r_{m}), which is cheaper than saving previous iterates if we choose rm<rr_{m}<r. We compare against LoFT’s momentum mechanism in Table 1 and show that our LoRSum-based momentum can outperform SVDLoRA under large enough rank budgets. We show in Algorithm 2 the the PSI-LoRA step with LoRSum momentum. More details are provided in Appendix E.

4 Beyond SGD: F-LoRSum with Kronecker-factored metrics

We now extend LoRSum to handle Kronecker-factored metrics. Specifically, we consider the K-FAC metric, which approximates the Fisher information matrix. Thus, we call our method Fisher-metric LoRSum (F-LoRSum). The procedure is described in Algorithm 6, which implements a preconditioned PSI-LoRA step with F-LoRSum. For notational simplicity, Algorithm 6 does not detail how to perform the multiplications efficiently. We provide the full details Appendix E.

4.1 LoRSum with Kronecker-factored metrics

We can endow the proximal terms in 9 with non-Euclidean metrics that can recover K-FAC and Shampoo updates. Let 𝐃𝐔≻0\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}\succ 0 and 𝐃𝐕≻0\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}\succ 0 define the weighted Frobenius norm

‖𝐖‖UV2:=⟨𝐖,𝐃𝐔​𝐖𝐃𝐕⟩F.\|\mathbf{W}\|_{\mathrm{UV}}^{2}:=\langle\mathbf{W},\,\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}\rangle_{\mathrm{F}}.

Similarly, we can define ‖𝐔‖𝐔2:=⟨𝐔,𝐃𝐔​𝐔⟩F\|\mathbf{U}\|_{\mathbf{U}}^{2}:=\langle\mathbf{U},\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}\mathbf{U}\rangle_{\mathrm{F}} and ‖𝐕‖𝐕2:=⟨𝐕,𝐃𝐕​𝐕⟩F\|\mathbf{V}\|_{\mathbf{V}}^{2}:=\langle\mathbf{V},\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}\mathbf{V}\rangle_{\mathrm{F}}. By Cauchy-Schwarz, we have ‖𝐔𝐕⊤‖UV≤‖𝐔‖𝐔​‖𝐕‖𝐕\|\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}\|_{\mathrm{UV}}\leq\|\mathbf{U}\|_{\mathbf{U}}\,\|\mathbf{V}\|_{\mathbf{V}}, so these norms are consistent.

To simplify derivations, we define the linear operator

D⁡(𝐖):=𝐃𝐔​𝐖​𝐃𝐕,D(\mathbf{W}):=\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}\,\mathbf{W}\,\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}},

so that ‖𝐖‖UV2=‖D1/2​(𝐖)‖F2\|\mathbf{W}\|_{\mathrm{UV}}^{2}=\|D^{1/2}(\mathbf{W})\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}. Now, consider preconditioning a step Δt\Delta_{t}, e.g., Δt=−η⁡(𝐆t+α​ℳt−1)\Delta_{t}=-\eta(\mathbf{G}_{t}+\alpha\mathcal{M}_{t-1}), so that

𝐖~t+1=𝐖t+D−1​(Δt)=𝐖t+𝐃𝐔−1​Δt​𝐃𝐕−1.\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}=\mathbf{W}_{t}+D^{-1}(\Delta_{t})=\mathbf{W}_{t}+\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}^{-1}\Delta_{t}\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}^{-1}.

The reason we call 𝐃𝐔\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}} and 𝐃𝐕\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}} Kronecker-factored metrics is because of the following identity

vec⁡(𝐃𝐔​𝐖𝐃𝐕)=(𝐃𝐕⊤⊗𝐃𝐔)​vec⁡(𝐖),\vecop(\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}})=(\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}^{\top}\otimes\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}})\vecop(\mathbf{W}),

where ⊗\otimes is the Kronecker product and vec⁡(⋅)\vecop(\cdot) is the vectorization operator. Thus, preconditioned gradient descent under the metric ∥⋅∥UV\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{UV}} is equivalent to standard gradient descent under the Kronecker-factored preconditioner 𝐃𝐕⊗𝐃𝐔\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}\otimes\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}} for symmetric 𝐃𝐔\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}} and 𝐃𝐕\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}. Indeed, the metric rank-rr projection of 𝐖~t+1\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1} is

ΠrUV​(𝐖~t+1)∈arg​minrank⁡(𝐖)≤r⁡‖𝐖−𝐖~t+1‖UV2,\Pi_{r}^{\mathrm{UV}}(\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1})\in\argmin_{\rank(\mathbf{W})\leq r}\|\mathbf{W}-\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\|_{\mathrm{UV}}^{2},

and since multiplication by invertible matrices preserves rank, we directly get

ΠrUV(𝐖~t+1)=D−1/2(Πr(D1/2(𝐖~t+1))).\Pi_{r}^{\mathrm{UV}}(\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1})=D^{-1/2}(\Pi_{r}(D^{1/2}(\tilde{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}))).

We can interpret metric projections as running LoRSum in whitened space and then unwhitening the output factors.

Thus, we can write the effective proximal subproblem under the metric rank-rr projection as

min𝐔,𝐕\displaystyle\min_{\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}} ⟨𝐔𝐕⊤,Δt⟩F+12​‖𝐔𝐕⊤−𝐖t‖UV2\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top},\Delta_{t}\rangle_{\mathrm{F}}+\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}-\mathbf{W}_{t}\|^{2}_{\text{UV}} (13)
+ρ2​‖𝐔−𝐔t‖U2+ρ2​‖𝐕−𝐕t‖V2.\displaystyle+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\mathbf{U}-\mathbf{U}_{t}\|^{2}_{\text{U}}+\frac{\rho}{2}\|\mathbf{V}-\mathbf{V}_{t}\|^{2}_{\text{V}}.

Note the the inner product is Euclidean. Same as before, the first-order optimality conditions give fixed-point equations, for which the Gauss-Seidel iterations will yield the following updates,

𝐔(k+1)\displaystyle\mathbf{U}^{(k+1)} =(𝐔𝐕⊤​𝐃𝐕​𝐕(k)+ρ​𝐔+𝐃𝐔−1​Δt​𝐕(k))\displaystyle=\big(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}+\rho\mathbf{U}+\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}^{-1}\Delta_{t}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}\big) (14)
⋅((𝐕(k))⊤​𝐃𝐕​𝐕(k)+ρ​𝐈r)−1,\displaystyle\cdot\big((\mathbf{V}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}+\rho\mathbf{I}_{r}\big)^{-1},
𝐕(k+1)\displaystyle\mathbf{V}^{(k+1)} =(𝐕𝐔⊤​𝐃𝐔​𝐔(k+1)+ρ​𝐕+𝐃𝐕−1​Δt⊤​𝐔(k+1))\displaystyle=\big(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}\mathbf{U}^{(k+1)}+\rho\mathbf{V}+\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}^{-1}\Delta_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}^{(k+1)}\big)
⋅((𝐔(k+1))⊤​𝐃𝐔​𝐔(k+1)+ρ​𝐈r)−1.\displaystyle\cdot\big((\mathbf{U}^{(k+1)})^{\top}\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}\mathbf{U}^{(k+1)}+\rho\mathbf{I}_{r}\big)^{-1}.

We refer to this variant as F-LoRSum (Fisher LoRSum) since we consider K-FAC, which is an approximation of the Fisher information metric.

Diagonal K-FAC for memory-efficiency.

Natural gradient descent (Amari, 1998) is a powerful algorithm, but it is often intractable for large models because computing the Fisher information matrix is prohibitively expensive. Kronecker-factored approximations such as K-FAC (Martens & Grosse, 2020) make this scaling practical and are widely used in practice. The K-FAC statistics for 𝐃𝐔\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}} and 𝐃𝐕\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}} are given by

𝐃𝐔\displaystyle\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}} =𝔼⁡[𝐬t​𝐬t⊤]≈1B​𝐒t⊤​𝐒t,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{s}_{t}\mathbf{s}_{t}^{\top}]\approx\frac{1}{B}\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{S}_{t},
𝐃𝐕\displaystyle\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}} =𝔼⁡[𝐱t​𝐱t⊤]≈1B​𝐗t⊤​𝐗t,\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{x}_{t}\mathbf{x}_{t}^{\top}]\approx\frac{1}{B}\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t},

where 𝐱t\mathbf{x}_{t} is a random input vector and 𝐬t\mathbf{s}_{t} is the corresponding gradient w.r.t. the layer outputs. For large models, storing dense 𝐃𝐔\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}} and 𝐃𝐕\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}} defeats the very purpose of using low-rank adapters. We therefore use diagonal K-FAC metrics,

𝐃𝐔≈diag⁡(𝐯𝐬),𝐃𝐕≈diag⁡(𝐯𝐱),\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}\approx\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{s}}),\quad\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}\approx\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{x}}),

where 𝐯𝐬∈ℝdout\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{s}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}} and 𝐯𝐱∈ℝdin\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{in}}} are exponential moving average (EMA) estimates of per-coordinate second moments computed from 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} and 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t}. We can similarly use Shampoo-style statistics (Gupta et al., 2018) as we show in Section E.2.

Fractional metrics.

A nice property of Kronecker products is that they are closed under fractional powers, i.e., (𝐃𝐕⊗𝐃𝐔)γ=𝐃𝐕γ⊗𝐃𝐔γ(\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}\otimes\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}})^{\gamma}=\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}^{\gamma}\otimes\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}^{\gamma} for any γ>0\gamma>0. In general, one can choose any γ∈(0,1]\gamma\in(0,1], which interpolates between first-order updates and natural-gradient scaling. Inspired by the success of Shampoo-style γ=1/4\gamma=1/4 powers (Shi et al., 2023), we use a fractional power γ=12\gamma=\tfrac{1}{2} for K-FAC in our experiments. In fact, this square-root K-FAC enjoys an interesting property: the preconditioned gradient step has a Frobenius norm bounded by min⁡{rank⁡(𝐒),rank⁡(𝐗)}\min\{\rank(\mathbf{S}),\rank(\mathbf{X})\} up to damping. This fact is easy to show, but we defer it to Appendix D for brevity. We believe this can act as a form of soft gradient normalization, which is likely the reason why we can use very large learning rates.

5 Experiments

In all our experiments, linear layers are frozen and adapters are added. The rest of the model parameters, if any, are trained normally. We consider a linear task, image classification on CIFAR-100 (Krizhevsky, 2009), GLUE text classification tasks (Wang et al., 2019), SQuAD v2 question answering tasks (Rajpurkar et al., 2018), and language modeling on WikiText-103 (Merity et al., 2016). We also ablate the parameters of Scaled PSI-LoRA on GLUE-MNLI to show its robustness. All experiments use rank r=8r=8 adapters, except CIFAR-100 which uses r=16r=16. We fine-tune query and value projection layers in GLUE and SQuAD tasks. We implement all methods in PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019) and use the Hugging Face’s PEFT (Mangrulkar et al., 2022) and fine-tuning scripts as the base code for the language model LoRA experiments.

Baselines. We consider the following tuning baselines: Full-weight, LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), Riemannian Preconditioned LoRA (RPLoRA) (Zhang & Pilanci, 2024; Tong et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021), SVDLoRA, PSI-LoRA with LoRSum momentum (Algorithm 2), PSI-LoRA with LoFT’s projected momentum (Proj. PSI-LoRA) (Tastan et al., 2025), and scaled PSI-LoRA with diagonal K-FAC metrics (F-LoRSum). We consider using both SGD or AdamW optimizers (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) for Full-weight, LoRA, RPLoRA, and SVDLoRA. AdamW always uses the default parameters with zero weight decay unless otherwise stated. For non-LoRA parameters, we use SGD with momentum for non-scaled PSI-LoRA and AdamW for Scaled PSI-LoRA. Note that SVDLoRA maintains full-rank optimization states, such as momentum or second moment in AdamW. For PSI-LoRA and its scaled variant on CIFAR-100, we consider different number of inner alternating iterations KK and use the notation "PSI-LoRA ×K\times K". For language model experiments, we consider simultaneous updates with K=1K=1.

Linear task. The linear task is as simple as 2; we consider the objective min𝐔,𝐕⁡12​‖𝐔𝐕⊤−𝐖‖F2\min_{\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}}\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}-\mathbf{W}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2} with 𝐖∈ℝ600×200\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{600\times 200}. The full-batch task uses SGD without momentum, and mini-batch samples columns (batch size 64) and uses momentum α=0.75\alpha=0.75.

In the full-batch case, SVDLoRA converges in one step with η=1\eta=1, and we use the same η\eta for PSI-LoRA. In Figure 1, we show how PSI-LoRA converges to SVDLoRA as K→∞K\to\infty. In the stochastic setting, PSI-LoRA outperforms SVDLoRA for small KK, and larger KK tracks SVDLoRA more closely but can plateau earlier. This counter-intuitive behavior suggests that SVDLoRA’s local optimality (Proposition 1) may not always translate to better generalization in stochastic settings, despite maintaining full-rank momentum.

CIFAR-100 task. For CIFAR-100, we use a custom MLP with one convolution layer that transforms the input into patches, and then we process the patches using linear layers throughout. Further, we initialize LoRAs with SVDLoRA of the base layers’ weights, and then set the base layers to zero. This task serves as a stress-test of LoRA methods and a proof of concept for PSI-LoRA. We start noticing in this task that increasing the number of inner iterations KK does not necessarily improve performance. Results are shown in Table 2.

RoBERTa on GLUE. We demonstrate the feasibility of Scaled PSI-LoRA on a real-world sequence classification fine-tuning task. Training is done via a tweaked fine-tuning script from Hugging Face. We use RoBERTa (Liu et al., 2019) for sequence classification on GLUE tasks (Wang et al., 2019). We consider the tasks MNLI, QNLI, QQP, SST-2, CoLA, and STS-B. We tune on  20% training budget (with a constant schedule) over 3 learning rates, and pick the overall best performing hyper-parameters across all tasks. The values in Table 1 are reported for the same learning rate per method (see Figure 6 for full learning curves and learning rates). For example, for Scaled PSI-LoRA, we set η=0.2\eta=0.2, β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.99\beta_{2}=0.99, δ=10−5\delta=10^{-5}, K=1K=1 (simultaneous), and ρ=0.01\rho=0.01, which we found to be fairly tranferable across other tasks as well, where tuning β2\beta_{2} can sometimes give further improvements.

The reason we set the same learning rate across tasks of varying sizes and difficulties is to check the robustness of the optimizers and how much tuning is required in practice. This is especially evident for CoLA, as the hyperparameters are not tuned specifically for it. Also, RPLoRA’s learning rate does not generalize well as can be seen from its large variance on QNLI, for example.

T5 on SQuAD v2. We also show that Scaled PSI-LoRA perform well on a seq2seq task using T5 (Raffel et al., 2020) fine-tuned on SQuAD v2 (Rajpurkar et al., 2018). We similarly tune over 3 learning rates per method and consider full training budget. See Appendix F for more details.

GPT-2 on WikiText-103. This is a language modeling task where we fine-tune GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) on WikiText-103 (Merity et al., 2016) with LoRA adapters. We show that Scaled PSI-LoRA is much more robust than LoRA and SVDLoRA across a search over 3 learning rates, i.e., {1e-4, 2e-4, 5e-4} for LoRA and SVDLoRA, and {0.5, 1.0, 2.0} for Scaled PSI-LoRA. Scaled PSI-LoRA achieves better perplexity no matter which learning rate we set. The results are shown in Figure 2.

Ablation of Scaled PSI-LoRA. In order to further stress-test Scaled PSI-LoRA we test various hyperparameters on GLUE-MNLI given a fixed (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.99)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.99). We compare Scaled PSI-LoRA with metric powers γ∈{0.25,0.5}\gamma\in\{0.25,0.5\}, use a K-FAC vs. Shampoo statistics, and consider damping δ∈{10−1,10−3,10−5,10−8}\delta\in\{10^{-1},10^{-3},10^{-5},10^{-8}\}. Results are shown in Figure 3. We observe that K-FAC performs best with γ=0.5\gamma=0.5 and lower damping δ≤10−5\delta\leq 10^{-5}, and it is quite robust to the choice of δ\delta. Shampoo statistics perform well when γ=0.25\gamma=0.25, but we do not see a clear advantage over K-FAC. Most interestingly, we see that Scaled PSI-LoRA can perform well for a surprisingly wide range of learning rates, ranging from 0.010.01 to 10.010.0. This supports the claim that Scaled PSI-LoRA decreases the burden of learning rate tuning significantly.

6 Discussion and Limitations

PSI-LoRA trades extra per-step compute for avoiding full-matrix SVD projections, while remaining robust across a wide range of learning rates and hyperparameters. The main limitations are: (i) overhead incurred from caching inputs and gradients w.r.t outputs and running inner iterations, (ii) larger KK can degrade under stochastic gradients, even on simple tasks (Figure 1), but this is also true for the SVDLoRA oracle, and (iii) diagonal Kronecker metrics are memory-efficient but crude.

We have experimented with several directions to improve PSI-LoRA and F-LoRSum that we leave to future work: (i) using low-rank metrics instead of diagonal and updating them with LoRSum, (ii) memory-efficient gradient accumulation with 𝐗\mathbf{X} and 𝐒\mathbf{S} and sketching using LoRSum, (iii) mitigating the stochastic sensitivity with variance reduction (Cutkosky & Orabona, 2019) or with more principled momentum schemes (Beck & Teboulle, 2009), and (iv) reducing runtime with a distributed implementation (Shi et al., 2023).

Impact Statement

This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of Machine Learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.

Appendix A Additional implementation details

A.1 LoRSum technical details

Caching activations for inner iterations.

To support K>1K>1 inner iterations, we cache the exact layer inputs 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t} and output gradients 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} that define the per-layer gradient 𝐆t=𝐒t⊤​𝐗t\mathbf{G}_{t}=\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}. This is required because the inner iterations access products of the form 𝐆t​𝐕(k)=𝐒t⊤​(𝐗t​𝐕(k))\mathbf{G}_{t}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}=\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{t}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}) and 𝐆t⊤​𝐔(k)=𝐗t⊤​(𝐒t​𝐔(k))\mathbf{G}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}^{(k)}=\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}(\mathbf{S}_{t}\mathbf{U}^{(k)}) for updated factors. With dropout, gradient clipping, loss scaling, or gradient accumulation, 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t} and 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} must correspond to the post-dropout / post-scaling quantities used in the backward pass. Otherwise, recomputed products such as 𝐆t​𝐕(k)\mathbf{G}_{t}\mathbf{V}^{(k)} become inconsistent with the gradient that autograd applied. In our implementation, we apply clipping and loss-scaling consistently to the cached 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t} and 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t}, used by inner iterations and metric updates.

Mixed precision and loss scaling.

When using AMP with dynamic loss scaling (e.g. GradScaler), 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} is produced in scaled units. Before using cached activations for inner iterations or updating curvature statistics, we unscale 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} by the current scale factor so that 𝐆t=𝐒t⊤​𝐗t\mathbf{G}_{t}=\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t} matches the true gradient. Equivalently, one can keep 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} in scaled units as long as the same convention is used consistently for (i) the update term and (ii) any metric / second-moment statistics derived from 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t}. With gradient accumulation, 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} should reflect the same averaging convention as the final accumulated gradient (e.g., mean over accumulated mini-batches).

Choosing ρ\rho and δ\delta.

We found that it is best to tune a reparameterization of the proximal parameter θ=ρ/η\theta=\rho/\eta. In our experiments, we found that θ∈[10−3,10−2]\theta\in[10^{-3},10^{-2}] to be a good range across tasks and optimizers. We also consider ρ=θ​ηt\rho=\theta\eta_{t}, where ηt\eta_{t} follows a learning rate schedule, which also works even as ηt→0\eta_{t}\to 0, but we set a lower bound on ρ>10−5\rho>10^{-5} to avoid ill-conditioning in the inner systems. Compare this with AdamW’s weight decay (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019), which is also scaled by the learning rate.

We also use δ\delta for metric damping in scaled variants, which is an important recipe for the stabilizing the K-FAC optimizer. However, we found that our algorithm, with γ=1/2\gamma=1/2, is surprisingly resilient to low damping values, which is not the case when γ=1\gamma=1. We show the plots of the ablation experiments in Figure 3.

Solving the inner systems.

Since all solves / inverses involve symmetric positive definite matrices, we use Cholesky factorization followed by triangular solves. In case of failures, the solver falls back to more general and stabler solves. However, we rarely observed such failures in practice that are not due to bad hyperparameter settings. In general, we solve the r×rr\times r systems in FP32 without inversion.

A.2 Gradient clipping

When using gradient clipping by global norm, we considered applying the clipping factor to either 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t}, 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t}, split the scale evenly across both. Importantly, we update curvature statistics with the clipped factors ca​𝐗tc^{a}\mathbf{X}_{t} and c1−a​𝐒tc^{1-a}\mathbf{S}_{t} for some a∈[0,1]a\in[0,1], which noticeably improved performance. This suggests that gradient clipping’s usefulness is in robustifying samples of 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t} and 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} and not only bounding updates within a trust-region.

We found that setting a=1a=1, i.e., applying the clipping factor fully to 𝐗t\mathbf{X}_{t}, worked best in practice, which made sense since we found that ‖𝐗t‖≫‖𝐒t‖\|\mathbf{X}_{t}\|\gg\|\mathbf{S}_{t}\| typically (even after accounting for the 1/B1/B scaling in 𝐒t\mathbf{S}_{t} from averaging the loss). However, this is also surprising because the gradient clipping, which we found to be crucial for stable training, almost cancels out in the final update in when disabling EMA (β1=β2=0\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=0) and using γ=1/2\gamma=1/2.

To see this, let us consider the clipped inputs c​𝐗tc\mathbf{X}_{t} for c≤1c\leq 1 and set δ≈0\delta\approx 0 and γ=1/2\gamma=1/2. Next, set the K-FAC statistics with these clipped inputs so that the metrics become

𝐃𝐔=(𝐒t⊤​𝐒t)1/2,𝐃𝐕=c​(𝐗t⊤​𝐗t)1/2,\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}=(\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{S}_{t})^{1/2},\qquad\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}=c(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t})^{1/2},

Take the F-LoRSum iterations 14. The shrinkage term will clearly cancel out the scaling in both updates. However, taking the effective preconditioned steps 𝐆~𝐔\tilde{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{U}} and 𝐆~𝐕\tilde{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{V}}, we have

𝐆~𝐔\displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{U}} =(𝐒t⊤𝐒t)−1/2𝐆t𝐕(𝐕⊤(𝐗t⊤𝐗t)1/2𝐕+ρc−1𝐈)−1\displaystyle=(\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{S}_{t})^{-1/2}\mathbf{G}_{t}\mathbf{V}\big(\mathbf{V}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t})^{1/2}\mathbf{V}+\rho{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}c^{-1}}\mathbf{I}\big)^{-1}
𝐆~𝐕\displaystyle\tilde{\mathbf{G}}_{\mathbf{V}} =(𝐗t⊤𝐗t)−1/2𝐆t⊤𝐔(𝐔⊤(𝐒t⊤𝐒t)1/2𝐔+ρ𝐈)−1.\displaystyle=(\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t})^{-1/2}\mathbf{G}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}\big(\mathbf{U}^{\top}(\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{S}_{t})^{1/2}\mathbf{U}+\rho\mathbf{I}\big)^{-1}.

This interesting scale-invariance property follows from the half-Fisher preconditioning using K-FAC statistics, which is easy to prove, as we show in Appendix D. However, there is also an implicit increase of the proximal term by c−1≥1c^{-1}\geq 1 in the 𝐔\mathbf{U} update, which may offer a different perspective on choosing ρ\rho adaptively based on the gradient norm since c−1∝‖∇f​(𝐖t)‖c^{-1}\propto\|\nabla f(\mathbf{W}_{t})\| when it is active.

Indeed, such adaptive damping strategies have long been studied under the lens of differential equations as Hessian-driven damping (Alvarez, 2000; Attouch et al., 2014; Su et al., 2016), and recently in the context of adaptive optimization methods but with ‖∇f​(𝐖t)‖\sqrt{\|\nabla f(\mathbf{W}_{t})\|} instead (Zhang et al., 2021; Mishchenko, 2023). However, we are not aware of connections between Hessian damping and gradient clipping in deep learning.

In general, our exact method does not fully cancel out the clipping effect since typically we have β1,β2≥0.9\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\geq 0.9. Nonetheless, the above analysis suggests that clipping has a more subtle effect than just bounding the step size.

A.3 Distributed data-parallel training

Let us assume that the loss is a mean over BB samples per step. In data-parallel training with RR workers, the effective step should then use the global mean gradient

𝐆t=1R​∑r=1R𝐆r,t,𝐆r,t=𝐒r,t⊤​𝐗r,t,\mathbf{G}_{t}=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\mathbf{G}_{r,t},\qquad\mathbf{G}_{r,t}=\mathbf{S}_{r,t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{r,t},

where 𝐗r,t\mathbf{X}_{r,t} and 𝐒r,t\mathbf{S}_{r,t} are the local inputs and output gradients on worker rr. Standard LoRA updates only require 𝐆t​𝐕t\mathbf{G}_{t}\mathbf{V}_{t} and 𝐆t⊤​𝐔t\mathbf{G}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}_{t}, which autograd computes and DDP synchronizes automatically. However, our inner iterations require products with updated factors, 𝐆t​𝐕(k)\mathbf{G}_{t}\mathbf{V}^{(k)} and 𝐆t⊤​𝐔(k)\mathbf{G}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}^{(k)}, which are not part of the autograd graph.

To obtain consistent inner-iteration updates across workers, we compute these products locally and all-reduce the resulting thin matrices

𝐆t​𝐕(k)=1R​∑r=1R(𝐒r,t)⊤​(𝐗r,t​𝐕(k)),𝐆t⊤​𝐔(k)=1R​∑r=1R(𝐗r,t)⊤​(𝐒r,t​𝐔(k)).\mathbf{G}_{t}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}(\mathbf{S}_{r,t})^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{r,t}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}),\qquad\mathbf{G}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{U}^{(k)}\;=\;\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}(\mathbf{X}_{r,t})^{\top}(\mathbf{S}_{r,t}\mathbf{U}^{(k)}).

Both all-reduced quantities have shapes dout×rd_{\mathrm{out}}\times r and din×rd_{\mathrm{in}}\times r, so the communication cost is modest compared to synchronizing full gradients. Note that this applies to LoRSum momentum updates as well.

Synchronizing diagonal Kronecker statistics.

For scaled variants using diagonal Kronecker factors (e.g. diagonal K-FAC/Shampoo-style), we also all-reduce the per-step diagonal statistics (e.g. diag⁡(1B​𝐗r,t⊤​𝐗r,t)\mathrm{diag}(\tfrac{1}{B}\mathbf{X}_{r,t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{r,t}) and diag⁡(1B​𝐒r,t⊤​𝐒r,t)\mathrm{diag}(\tfrac{1}{B}\mathbf{S}_{r,t}^{\top}\mathbf{S}_{r,t})) before updating the EMA. Without this step, each worker solves a different projection subproblem and parameters may drift.

Appendix B Proofs

B.1 Proof of Theorem 3.1

Theorem 3.1 (restated).

Consider the iterations 10, where 𝐖¯t+1=𝐔t(0)​𝐕t(0)−η​𝐆t\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}=\mathbf{U}_{t}^{(0)}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{(0)}-\eta\mathbf{G}_{t} and ρ=0\rho=0. Assume span⁡(𝐕(0))\mathspan(\mathbf{V}^{(0)}) has nonzero overlap with the top-rr right singular subspace of 𝐖¯t+1\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}. Let σ1≥…​σmin⁡{din,dout}\sigma_{1}\geq\ldots\sigma_{\min\{d_{\text{in}},d_{\text{out}}\}} be the singular values of 𝐖¯t+1\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1} and let 𝐖t+1svd=Πr​(𝐖¯t+1)\mathbf{W}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{svd}}=\Pi_{r}(\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}) be its best rank-rr approximation. Then, for some constant C>0C>0 that depends on the initialization 𝐕t(0)\mathbf{V}_{t}^{(0)}, we have that

‖𝐔t(k)​𝐕t(k)−𝐖t+1svd‖F2≤C​(σr+1σr)2​k.\|\mathbf{U}_{t}^{(k)}\mathbf{V}_{t}^{(k)}-\mathbf{W}_{t+1}^{\mathrm{svd}}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\leq C\left(\frac{\sigma_{r+1}}{\sigma_{r}}\right)^{2k}.
Proof.

The iterations 5 satisfy alternating projections following 11, giving

span⁡(𝐔t+1(k+1))=span⁡(𝐖¯t+1​𝐕t+1(k))=span⁡(𝐖¯t+1​𝐖¯t+1⊤​𝐔t+1(k)),\displaystyle\mathspan(\mathbf{U}_{t+1}^{(k+1)})=\mathspan(\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\mathbf{V}_{t+1}^{(k)})=\mathspan(\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}^{\top}\mathbf{U}_{t+1}^{(k)}), (15)

which is a block power iteration on 𝐖¯t+1​𝐖¯t+1⊤\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}^{\top}. By symmetry, span⁡(𝐕t+1(k+1))=span⁡(𝐖¯t+1⊤​𝐖¯t+1​𝐕t+1(k))\mathspan(\mathbf{V}_{t+1}^{(k+1)})=\mathspan(\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}^{\top}\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\mathbf{V}_{t+1}^{(k)}), which is a block power iteration on 𝐖¯t+1⊤​𝐖¯t+1\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}^{\top}\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}. This is exactly a subspace iteration method (Saad, 2011; Gu, 2014), so the convergence in Frobenius norm follows. ∎

Remark B.1.

In subspace iteration, the iterates are orthonormalized, which amounts to taking the inverse square roots in 10. In other words, the multiplications 𝐖¯t+1​𝐖¯t+1⊤\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}^{\top} and 𝐖¯t+1⊤​𝐖¯t+1\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}^{\top}\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1} are explicitly done, whereas they are implicitly done via alternating ALS updates.

Remark B.2.

The assumption required for span⁡(𝐕(0))\mathspan(\mathbf{V}^{(0)}) is mild in practice since we warm-start from the previous step’s factors. Also, at LoRA initialization 𝐕0\mathbf{V}_{0} is a Gaussian matrix, which satisfies this assumption almost surely. This also suggests that the order we adopt in 5 and 10 is preferable for LoRA training, and that random initializations for 𝐕\mathbf{V} can be used in other applications of LoRSum.

Appendix C Interpretations of the proximal projection

This appendix records two complementary ways to view the proximal subproblem in 9.

(i) A stabilized approximation to the rank-rr projection.

Let 𝐖¯t+1=𝐖t−η​𝐆t\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}=\mathbf{W}_{t}-\eta\mathbf{G}_{t} denote the full step before projection. The proximal factor projection solves

min𝐔,𝐕⁡12​‖𝐔𝐕⊤−𝐖¯t+1‖F2+ρ2​(‖𝐔−𝐔t‖F2+‖𝐕−𝐕t‖F2).\min_{\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}}\ \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}-\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}+\frac{\rho}{2}\big(\|\mathbf{U}-\mathbf{U}_{t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}+\|\mathbf{V}-\mathbf{V}_{t}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\big).

This interpretation follows by the construction of the sub-problem as a proximal approximation to the idealized rank-rr projection step. When ρ=0\rho=0 and the inner solve is exact and the objective reduces to minrank⁡(𝐖)≤r⁡‖𝐖−𝐖¯t+1‖F2\min_{\rank(\mathbf{W})\leq r}\|\mathbf{W}-\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}, whose solution is the truncated SVD projection Πr​(𝐖¯t+1)\Pi_{r}(\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}), i.e., the SVDLoRA oracle. For ρ>0\rho>0 and a finite number of ALS iterations, the proximal terms select a particular factorization that stays close to (𝐔t,𝐕t)(\mathbf{U}_{t},\mathbf{V}_{t}), which improves stability in deep networks while still tracking the same rank-rr projection in the limit.

(ii) Lifted-space proximal step under a non-linear constraint.

Define the lifted variable 𝐳=vec⁡(𝐖,ρ​𝐔,ρ​𝐕)\mathbf{z}=\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{W},\sqrt{\rho}\mathbf{U},\sqrt{\rho}\mathbf{V}) and 𝐳t=vec⁡(𝐖t,ρ​𝐔t,ρ​𝐕t)\mathbf{z}_{t}=\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{W}_{t},\sqrt{\rho}\mathbf{U}_{t},\sqrt{\rho}\mathbf{V}_{t}). Then, the above problem is the proximal map of the linearized model of ff in the lifted space, with the non-linear constraint 𝐖=𝐔𝐕⊤\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top} enforced by restricting to feasible (𝐖,𝐔,𝐕)(\mathbf{W},\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}). We can write the proximal step as

min𝐳⁡⟨∇𝐖f​(𝐳t),𝐖−𝐖t⟩+12​η​‖𝐳−𝐳t‖22+𝟏𝐖=𝐔𝐕⊤​(𝐳),\min_{\mathbf{z}}\ \langle\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}f(\mathbf{z}_{t}),\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{W}_{t}\rangle+\frac{1}{2\eta}\|\mathbf{z}-\mathbf{z}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}+\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}}(\mathbf{z}),

where 𝟏E​(𝐳)\mathbf{1}_{E}(\mathbf{z}) is the indicator function of the non-convex constraint EE on 𝐳\mathbf{z}. This interpretation connects to proximal methods for constrained optimization (Parikh & Boyd, 2014), where the non-convex constraint 𝐖=𝐔𝐕⊤\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top} is handled implicitly by solving over the factorized variables. This viewpoint also suggests possible extensions to other constraints on 𝐖\mathbf{W} (e.g., sparsity, quantization) via proximal terms in the lifted space, handling f⁡(𝐳)f(\mathbf{z}) directly without linearizing over 𝐖\mathbf{W}, or considering relaxations of the non-convex constraint.

Appendix D Square-root K-FAC yields implicit gradient normalization

This section describes the property that half-Fisher (square-root K-FAC) preconditioning yields implicit gradient normalization in the single-layer case.

Let 𝐆=𝐒⊤​𝐗\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{X} be a single-layer gradient. Set the metrics 𝐃𝐔=(𝐒⊤​𝐒)1/2\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}=(\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{S})^{1/2} and 𝐃𝐕=(𝐗⊤​𝐗)1/2\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}=(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{1/2}. Without loss of generality, set damping δ=0\delta=0, and consider the half-K-FAC metric update

𝐖←𝐖−η𝐃𝐔−1𝐆𝐃𝐕−1=𝐖−η(𝐒⊤𝐒)−1/2𝐒⊤𝐗(𝐗⊤𝐗)−1/2=𝐖−η𝐒^⊤𝐗^,\mathbf{W}\leftarrow\mathbf{W}-\eta\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}^{-1}\mathbf{G}\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}^{-1}=\mathbf{W}-\eta(\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{S})^{-1/2}\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1/2}=\mathbf{W}-\eta\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{X}},

where we defined the orthonormalized factors

𝐒^=𝐒(𝐒⊤𝐒)−1/2,𝐗^=𝐗(𝐗⊤𝐗)−1/2,\hat{\mathbf{S}}=\mathbf{S}(\mathbf{S}^{\top}\mathbf{S})^{-1/2},\qquad\hat{\mathbf{X}}=\mathbf{X}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{-1/2},

so that 𝐒^⊤​𝐒^=𝐈\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{S}}=\mathbf{I} and 𝐗^⊤​𝐗^=𝐈\hat{\mathbf{X}}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{X}}=\mathbf{I}. This immediately implies that

‖𝐒^‖F2=rank⁡(𝐒^)=rank⁡(𝐒),‖𝐗^‖F2=rank⁡(𝐗^)=rank⁡(𝐗).\|\hat{\mathbf{S}}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}=\rank(\hat{\mathbf{S}})=\rank(\mathbf{S}),\qquad\|\hat{\mathbf{X}}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}=\rank(\hat{\mathbf{X}})=\rank(\mathbf{X}).

Furthermore, define the preconditioned gradient 𝐆~=𝐒^⊤​𝐗^\tilde{\mathbf{G}}=\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{X}}. Its squared Frobenius norm can be expressed as

‖𝐆~‖F2=tr⁡(𝐗^⊤​𝐒^​𝐒^⊤​𝐗^)=tr⁡(𝒫𝐒​𝒫𝐗)≤min⁡{rank⁡(𝐒),rank⁡(𝐗)},\|\tilde{\mathbf{G}}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}=\tr(\hat{\mathbf{X}}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{S}}\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}\hat{\mathbf{X}})=\tr(\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{S}}\mathcal{P}_{\mathbf{X}})\leq\min\{\rank(\mathbf{S}),\rank(\mathbf{X})\},

where, typically, min⁡{rank⁡(𝐒),rank⁡(𝐗)}≤B\min\{\rank(\mathbf{S}),\rank(\mathbf{X})\}\leq B for many modern linear layers (since most layers have one side dimension larger than the batch size BB). This shows that half-metric (square-root) K-FAC preconditioning controls the step norm by subspace overlap, rather than by the raw magnitudes of 𝐗\mathbf{X} and 𝐒\mathbf{S}.

This property does not necessarily apply to the F-LoRSum updates in 14 due to the way the metrics are applied (assuming ρ=0\rho=0):

𝐔(k+1)\displaystyle\mathbf{U}^{(k+1)} =(𝐔𝐕⊤​𝐃𝐕​𝐕(k)+𝐃𝐔−1​Δ​𝐕(k))​((𝐕(k))⊤​𝐃𝐕​𝐕(k))−1\displaystyle=\big(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}+\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}^{-1}\Delta\mathbf{V}^{(k)}\big)\big((\mathbf{V}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}\big)^{-1}
=(𝐔𝐕⊤​(𝐗⊤​𝐗)1/2​𝐕(k)+𝐒^⊤​𝐗𝐕(k))​((𝐕(k))⊤​(𝐗⊤​𝐗)1/2​𝐕(k))−1,\displaystyle=\big(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{1/2}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}+\hat{\mathbf{S}}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}\big)\big((\mathbf{V}^{(k)})^{\top}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{1/2}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}\big)^{-1},

so the soft normalization property does not hold exactly unless (𝐕(k))⊤​(𝐗⊤​𝐗)1/2​𝐕(k)=((𝐕(k))⊤​𝐗⊤​𝐗𝐕(k))1/2(\mathbf{V}^{(k)})^{\top}(\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X})^{1/2}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}=\big((\mathbf{V}^{(k)})^{\top}\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X}\mathbf{V}^{(k)}\big)^{1/2}, which requires orthogonal 𝐕(k)\mathbf{V}^{(k)} and commuting 𝐗⊤​𝐗\mathbf{X}^{\top}\mathbf{X} and 𝐕(k)​(𝐕(k))⊤\mathbf{V}^{(k)}(\mathbf{V}^{(k)})^{\top}. Nonetheless, we still observe stability using large learning rates with F-LoRSum, which suggests that the implicit normalization property of K-FAC is still approximately preserved in our updates.

Appendix E Algorithms and PyTorch reference implementation

This appendix collects algorithms and a minimal reference implementation in PyTorch (Paszke et al., 2019). Note that the code itself does not need PyTorch’s autograd for the updates, but we use it for consistency and ease of integration with existing training pipelines.

In the paper, 𝐖=𝐔𝐕⊤\mathbf{W}=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{V}^{\top} with 𝐔∈ℝdout×r\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{out}}\times r} and 𝐕∈ℝdin×r\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{in}}\times r}. In the reference code, we store factors as (𝐕⊤,𝐔)(\mathbf{V}^{\top},\mathbf{U}), which makes sense when read as (weight_in, weight_out), where the weights maintain their original shape in PyTorch’s convention. We maintain the same notation for the metrics, for example, (𝐃𝐕,𝐃𝐔)(\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}},\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}), which is (input_metric, output_metric), which flows naturally from left to right.

E.1 LoRSum and PSI-LoRA

LoRSum and PSI-LoRA algorithms are summarized in Algorithms 5 and 4. A minimal reference implementation of LoRSum is provided in Figure 4, and an implementation for F-LoRSum is provided in Figure 5. The algorithms contain dense-matrix notation for clarity (tagged with “unmaterialized”), but the implementation only uses thin-matrix operations and never materializes full dout×dind_{\mathrm{out}}\times d_{\mathrm{in}} matrices, as shown in the reference code.

Momentum buffer update.

We apply momentum at the level of the (approximate) full-rank update and then project back to rank rmr_{m}. Concretely, we consider the full update matrix 𝐖¯t+1=𝐖t−η⁡(𝐆t+α​ℳt−1)\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1}=\mathbf{W}_{t}-\eta(\mathbf{G}_{t}+\alpha\mathcal{M}_{t-1}) and project it with LoRSum, while separately updating ℳt\mathcal{M}_{t} as a low-rank approximation of 𝐆t+α​ℳt−1\mathbf{G}_{t}+\alpha\mathcal{M}_{t-1}. This might seem redundant, but it is important since we do not separately project gradient and momentum but rather together. In other words, 𝐖¯t+1\bar{\mathbf{W}}_{t+1} is is represented as a sum of low-rank terms, each of which is at most rank rr, but collectively can potentially be of higher rank. LoRSum can project this sum back to rank rr directly without materializing the full matrix. We found this to be an important detail for achieving competitive performance and a distinguishing feature of PSI-LoRA.

For simplicity, we always set rm=rr_{m}=r, except in the linear task experiment Figure 7, where we explicitly compare momentum rank budgets.

E.2 F-LoRSum and scaled PSI-LoRA

Scaled PSI-LoRA step (Algorithm 6) is similar to PSI-LoRA step (Algorithm 4), except that it uses exponential moving averages and F-LoRSum for the update (not for the momentum). We fix the hyperparameters (K,ρ)(K,\rho) to be the same for both operators for simplicity.

Partially preconditioned low-rank sums.

Note that, in F-LoRSum (Algorithm 7), The low-rank sum is expressed as 𝐖~=c1​𝐔1​𝐕1⊤+𝐃𝐔−1​(∑j=2ncj​𝐔j​𝐕j⊤)​𝐃𝐕−1\tilde{\mathbf{W}}=c_{1}\mathbf{U}_{1}\mathbf{V}_{1}^{\top}+\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U}}^{-1}\big(\sum_{j=2}^{n}c_{j}\mathbf{U}_{j}\mathbf{V}_{j}^{\top}\big)\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V}}^{-1}, where the first term is the warm start and the remaining terms are preconditioned by the Kronecker factors and constitute the effective step Δ=∑j=2ncj​𝐔j​𝐕j⊤\Delta=\sum_{j=2}^{n}c_{j}\mathbf{U}_{j}\mathbf{V}_{j}^{\top}. In general, there is no reason to choose only one pair of factors such that 𝐖t=𝐔1​𝐕1⊤\mathbf{W}_{t}=\mathbf{U}_{1}\mathbf{V}_{1}^{\top}, but we maintain this convention as we have not found a useful case where 𝐖t\mathbf{W}_{t} itself is represented by multiple terms. However, this is quite plausible if we are considering a combination of previous iterates or multiple LoRA adapters in the update.

Diagonal Kronecker-factored metrics with fractional power

Scaled PSI-LoRA replaces the Euclidean proximal terms in 9 with Kronecker-structured metrics. In practice we use diagonal Kronecker factors derived from running averages of second moments, e.g. diagonal K-FAC statistics:

𝐯s,t=diag⁡(1B​𝐒t⊤​𝐒t),𝐯x,t=diag⁡(1B​𝐗t⊤​𝐗t),\mathbf{v}_{s,t}=\mathrm{diag}\left(\tfrac{1}{B}\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{S}_{t}\right),\qquad\mathbf{v}_{x,t}=\mathrm{diag}\left(\tfrac{1}{B}\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{X}_{t}\right),

where we initialize 𝐯s,0=𝟏\mathbf{v}_{s,0}=\mathbf{1} and 𝐯x,0=𝟏\mathbf{v}_{x,0}=\mathbf{1}.

In practice, we maintain EMA estimates of 𝐯s,t\mathbf{v}_{s,t} and 𝐯x,t\mathbf{v}_{x,t} and then form fractional metric factors with damping

𝐃𝐔,t:=(𝐯s,t+δ)γ,𝐃𝐕,t:=(𝐯x,t+δ)γ,\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U},t}:=(\mathbf{v}_{s,t}+\delta)^{\gamma},\qquad\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V},t}:=(\mathbf{v}_{x,t}+\delta)^{\gamma},

and pass (𝐃𝐔,t,𝐃𝐕,t)(\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{U},t},\mathbf{D}_{\mathbf{V},t}) into the F-LoRSum routine.

We also considered diagonal Shampoo-style statistics (Gupta et al., 2018) in the ablation experiments,

𝐯s,tshampoo=diag⁡(1B​𝐒t⊤​(𝐗t​𝐗t⊤)​𝐒t),𝐯x,tshampoo=diag⁡(1B​𝐗t⊤​(𝐒t​𝐒t⊤)​𝐗t),\mathbf{v}_{s,t}^{\text{shampoo}}=\mathrm{diag}\left(\tfrac{1}{B}\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}(\mathbf{X}_{t}\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top})\mathbf{S}_{t}\right),\qquad\mathbf{v}_{x,t}^{\text{shampoo}}=\mathrm{diag}\left(\tfrac{1}{B}\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top}(\mathbf{S}_{t}\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top})\mathbf{X}_{t}\right),

We have found Shampoo to be marginally better (when γ=1/4\gamma=1/4) but more expensive to compute. It requires two additional thin GEMM operations per step to compute 𝐗t​𝐗t⊤\mathbf{X}_{t}\mathbf{X}_{t}^{\top} and 𝐒t​𝐒t⊤\mathbf{S}_{t}\mathbf{S}_{t}^{\top}, which cost O⁡(B2​(din+dout))O(B^{2}(d_{\mathrm{in}}+d_{\mathrm{out}})). This can be prohibitive when the effective batch size BB is large, especially for long sequences in language models, so we decided to use K-FAC to maintain simplicity and efficiency.

Appendix F Additional experimental details

F.1 Linear-task momentum ablation

We ablate the effect of increasing the rank budget of the low-rank momentum buffer in Figure 7. We use the same setup as in the linear task experiment in Figure 1, with LoRA rank r=8r=8 and vary the momentum rank rm∈{r,2​r,4​r}r_{m}\in\{r,2r,4r\}. We observe that increasing the momentum rank makes PSI-LoRA closer to the SVDLoRA oracle, which suggests that a higher-rank momentum buffer can better capture the history of updates. However, this also means that PSI-LoRA would plateau faster, as the SVDLoRA oracle also plateaus.

Linear task tuning notes.

For LoRA, we typically found the scaling η=0.02\eta=0.02 to work best. For SVDLoRA in the stochastic setting, we tuned η\eta over the grid {1,2,5}×10i\{1,2,5\}\times 10^{i} for i∈{−2,−1,0,1}i\in\{-2,-1,0,1\} and momentum α∈{…,0.7,0.75,0.8,0.85,0.9,0.95}\alpha\in\{\dots,0.7,0.75,0.8,0.85,0.9,0.95\}, and found η=0.1\eta=0.1 and α=0.75\alpha=0.75 to perform best.

GLUE RoBERTa validation curves.

We show in Figure 6 the full validation curves for RoBERTa-base GLUE experiments corresponding to Table 1 in the main text. The learning rates are shown in the legend for each method.

Hyperparameters.

Unless stated otherwise, LoRA rank is r=8r=8 (CIFAR-100 uses r=16r=16). We tune learning rates per method on a log grid {1​e−4,2​e−4,5​e−4,1​e−3,2​e−3,5​e−3,…}\{1e-4,2e-4,5e-4,1e-3,2e-3,5e-3,\ldots\} where the range depends on the method. For example, our method typically uses much higher learning rates in {0.1,0.2,0.5,1.0}\{0.1,0.2,0.5,1.0\}, whereas LoRA typically uses {1​e−4,2​e−4,5​e−4,1​e−3}\{1e-4,2e-4,5e-4,1e-3\}, and full training uses {1​e−4,2​e−5,5​e−5,1​e−4}\{1e-4,2e-5,5e-5,1e-4\}. However, we tune over 3 learning rates (typically, the larger ones) per method due to compute constraints. We average over 3 seeds and report mean and standard deviation.
